title: GitHub - jaystewartuk/voce: Read Markdown and code aloud in your terminal, the way a person says it, with each language's real operator names.
excerpt: Read Markdown and code aloud in your terminal, the way a person says it, with each language's real operator names. - jaystewartuk/voce
content_html:
Markdown and code, read aloud, in your terminal.
Screen readers spell code out symbol by symbol. voce reads it the way the person next to you would say it,
with each language's real operator names, and lights up each word as it is spoken.

Hear it · Website · Install · Claude Code · Voices · Playlists

🔊 Hear it read: 53 seconds of voce reading micrograd's backward pass, with the words lit as they are spoken (or the MP3).

voce (Italian for "voice", said VOH-chay) reads Markdown to you in the terminal. It shows the page as it should look, with headings, bold, links, highlighted code and lined-up tables, and reads it the way a person would: the prose as prose, and the code the way a pairing partner says it out loud. You can look away, follow along, or jump around with the keyboard or the mouse.

Coding agents write a lot worth knowing: explanations of a codebase, walkthroughs of a pull request, lessons on a language or a framework. voce lets you listen to it instead of reading it, away from the screen if you like. Ask Claude Code, Codex or any agent to write you something, and press play. It reads any Markdown.

  • Reads code like a pairing partner. '1' === 1 is heard as "the string 1 is identical to 1", and $totals[$channel] ??= 0; as "totals channel null coalescing assignment zero". Operators get their manual's real names, in each language's own words, so you learn to say them. Thirteen languages so far: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust, PHP, Ruby, Java, C#, Swift, Kotlin, shell and SQL. See Code, read aloud.
  • Reads what a person would read. Markup is never spoken. Tables are read row by row, and links by their text. Things meant for the eye stay on the screen.
  • Follows along. The sentence being read sits on a pale band, and the word being spoken on a darker one. The page scrolls to keep your place, and a click on any sentence jumps there.
  • Knows Claude Code. voce -r reads Claude's latest reply in the folder you are in, with no copying.
  • Keeps your place. Quit at any point and it starts from the same sentence next time, even if the file has changed. It also reloads a file when it changes on disk.
  • Sounds good, costs nothing. Kokoro, a small open voice, runs on your computer out of the box: no account, no key, nothing sent anywhere. Every sentence is made once and cached, so listening again is instant.
  • Goes with you. --export turns files into one MP3 with the same voice and pauses, for a walk or a drive.

How it compares

Text-to-speech isn't new, and nor is having an agent's reply read out. What voce adds is code heard the way a person says it, with the page following along. Here is one line, $totals[$channel] ??= 0;, read four ways:

Reader What you hear On screen
Screen readers (VoiceOver, NVDA, Emacspeak) "dollar totals left bracket dollar channel right bracket question question equals zero semicolon", or the symbols skipped your editor, as it is
Read-aloud apps (Speechify, a browser's read aloud) the code read as prose, so Str::slug becomes "stress log" their own app
Agent read-aloud hooks and plugins usually "code omitted" nothing: audio only
voce "totals channel null coalescing assignment zero" the Markdown, styled, each word lit as it is spoken

voce is not a screen reader, and doesn't try to be one. It is for listening to things worth taking in: an agent's explanation, a pull request walkthrough, study notes on a language.

Install

You need macOS or Linux, and Python 3.10 to 3.14 for Kokoro, the voice that works out of the box. macOS's own python3 is 3.9, which gets only the Mac's voices, so name a newer one when you install (uv fetches it if you don't have it):

uv tool install --python 3.13 voce
# or
pipx install --python python3.13 voce

Then try it:

voce README.md

Two optional extras make it better:

  • The Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install) let voce build its small native audio player the first time it runs. You get gapless playback, a pause that keeps your place mid-word, and a word highlight that stays in time. Without them it falls back to afplay.
  • ffmpeg (brew install ffmpeg) is needed for --export.

On Linux, voce plays audio with mpv or ffplay if one is installed, else with pw-play, paplay or aplay, which play at one speed only. For the clipboard it uses wl-clipboard on Wayland, or xclip or xsel on X11:

sudo apt install mpv wl-clipboard      # or: sudo dnf install mpv wl-clipboard

On Windows, run it in WSL, where it is Linux.

Use it

voce notes.md              # read a file, from where you left off
voce a.md b.md             # read several files in a row
voce -r                    # read Claude Code's latest reply in this folder
voce -c                    # read what is on the clipboard
cat notes.md | voce -      # read standard input
voce                       # carry on with whatever you were last reading
voce --start notes.md      # start again from the top
voce notes.md --export notes.mp3   # one MP3 to take with you
voce --check notes.md      # how it will read: sentences, minutes, characters

Keys

Key Does
space pause or carry on
← → previous or next sentence
↑ ↓ previous or next paragraph
[ ] previous or next section
+ - faster or slower, from 0.8× to 2×
n p next or previous file
v next voice
V next voice engine, of those set up
m the playlist menu
r hear this sentence again, or the file again at the end
c C copy the sentence, or the whole paragraph
q quit, keeping your place

A click on a sentence or a line of code jumps to it. Drag across any text to copy it, without moving the voice: it is on the clipboard when you let go. With --skip-code, a click on a code block copies it. To select text with the terminal's own mouse instead, hold shift while you drag.

The mouse wheel scrolls, and the page follows the voice again at the next sentence. Vim users can use h j k l.

Every reader that speaks code gets it wrong in one of two ways. Screen readers read the symbols one by one: "dollar, totals, left bracket, dollar, channel...". Text-to-speech apps read code as if it were prose, and Str::slug comes out as "stress log". Neither says what a colleague sitting next to you would say.

voce reads code the way a pairing partner says it out loud, one line at a time, and the line sits on the band as it is read, with the word being spoken marked, just like a sentence of prose.

On the line What you hear
$totals[$channel] ??= 0; totals channel null coalescing assignment zero
usort($rows, fn ($a, $b) => $a['nights'] <=> $b['nights']); U sort rows, arrow function A, b returns A nights spaceship b nights
foreach ($rows as &$row) { for each rows as by reference row
'1' === 1; // false: a string is not an integer the string 1 is identical to 1, false: a string is not an integer
if (strpos($s, 'Hi') !== false) { ... } if string position s, Hi is not identical to false and so on
(int) (19.99 * 100); // 1998, a cent short cast to int 19.99 times 100, 1998, a cent short
Str::slug('Sea View'); string double colon slug Sea View
def __init__(self, **kwargs) -> None: (Python) def dunder init self, double star keyword args returns None
const name = user?.name ?? 'guest'; (JavaScript) const name equals user optional chaining name nullish coalescing guest
if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &v); err != nil { (Go) if error short variable declaration JSON dot Unmarshal data, address of v, error is not equal to nil
let n = reader.read(&mut buf)?; (Rust) let n equals reader dot read mutable borrow buffer try
name = user&.name || 'guest' (Ruby) name equals user safe navigation name or guest
val l = b?.length ?: 0 (Kotlin) val l equals b safe call length elvis zero
grep -r TODO src | wc -l && echo done (shell) grep dash r TODO source pipe W C dash l and then echo done
SELECT data->>'name' FROM users WHERE meta ? 'admin'; (SQL) SELECT data extracts as text name FROM users WHERE meta exists admin

The rules are the ones a person uses without thinking. Names are said as words: strlen is "string length", isset is "is set" and checkIn is "check In". Dollar signs, brackets and semicolons are silent. A string is read by its contents, so '' is "the empty string", and comments and doc comments are read as prose.

Operators get the names their language's manual gives them: PHP's === is "is identical to", not "triple equals", JavaScript's is "is strictly equal to", Go's := is "short variable declaration", Rust's ::< is "turbofish" and Kotlin's ?: is "elvis". Because the names are the real ones, you learn them as you listen, and they come out of your mouth when you pair or review code.

Each language is one file of words and operator names in speech/words/, naming the manual it follows, with tests that pin the exact words. Each was read through well-known projects in it with docs/hearing/corpus.py and checked by ear against the real voice. A fenced block is read in the language on its fence, a diff in the language of its file, and inline code in the language most of the document's code is in.

If you would rather hear only the prose, --skip-code shows code without reading it.

Use it with Claude Code

Keep Claude Code in one terminal and open a second one in the same folder. When a reply lands, run:

voce -r

voce finds the session for that folder in ~/.claude/projects. It reads the same text that /copy would take, which is Claude's final message without the progress notes, tool calls or thinking. If a turn is still running, it reads the previous reply.

You can also /copy the reply and run voce -c, which works in any terminal and with any tool.

Voices

Kokoro works out of the box. It is a small open voice model that runs on your computer, so it is free, needs no account and sends nothing anywhere. The first time it speaks, voce downloads the model (120 MB) into its cache. It needs Python 3.10 to 3.14; on 3.9, voce uses the Mac's own voices instead (on Linux, install a newer Python).

The Mac's voices are always there on macOS: voce --mac, or voce --mac --voice Daniel to pick one. Add better ones in System Settings, under Accessibility, Spoken Content, System voice, Manage voices.

Press v to move through an engine's voices and V to move to the other engine; both are remembered. Or name a voice and the engine follows: --voice bm_george (Kokoro) or --voice Daniel (the Mac). --engine picks an engine outright. If Kokoro fails part-way through, voce reads that sentence with the Mac's voice and tells you why. The full guide is in docs/voices.md.

Playlists and quizzes

A playlist is a README with a ## Listen in this order section that lists Markdown files, grouped into parts:

## Listen in this order

### Part 1. The basics
1. [Getting started](basics/start.md) · 12 min
2. [Core ideas](basics/ideas.md) · 9 min

Run voce --playlist path/to/folder once. After that, voce works through the files in order, voce --menu lets you choose one, and voce --list shows your progress. voce --prepare 1 fetches the audio for part 1 ahead of time, and voce --minutes updates the "· N min" figures.

A file with a numbered list under ## Quiz and the same number of answers under ## Answers becomes a quiz. voce reads a question, waits while you answer out loud, and reads the answer when you press space. voce --quiz runs just the quizzes. See docs/playlists.md.

What it understands

Headings, paragraphs, bold, italic, struck-through text, inline code, links and images all work. So do nested, numbered and task lists, block quotes and rules. Fenced code blocks are highlighted for every language Pygments knows, and long lines wrap instead of being cut off. Tables line up in columns, respect column alignment, and are read one row at a time.

It also handles a few things that suit listening. Anything inside <details> is shown but not read. Lines that are only links, such as breadcrumbs or "Next:" links, are shown but not read. Symbols such as →, ≈ and ×, and abbreviations such as "e.g." and "i.e.", are read as words.

Code, in fenced blocks and in sentences, is read the way a pairing partner says it: see Code, read aloud. A fenced diff block is highlighted with added lines in the file's syntax and removed lines in red, and read hunk by hunk: "Line 40", then the changed lines, with "Added" and "Removed" said once at the start of each run and the unchanged context shown but not read. Write the file's language after the word diff, as in ```diff python, to have the added lines highlighted and read in that language.

Pick up on another device

voce --sync you/voce keeps your places, settings and a prepared copy of each document in a private git repository of your own, so a second computer carries on where the first left off. A web app reads the same repository on a phone or in any browser, with a voice that runs in the page. There is no voce service: the repository is yours. See docs/sync.md.

Privacy

voce has no telemetry and makes no network calls of its own. What you read never leaves your computer: the only download is the Kokoro model, once, from GitHub. Everything voce keeps stays on your computer:

What Where
Your place in each document, one small file per document ~/.local/state/voce/places/
Speed, engine, voices and playlist ~/.local/state/voce/settings.json
Documents prepared for other devices ~/.local/state/voce/prepared/
The last 50 clipboard, reply and piped texts ~/.local/state/voce/clips/
Cached audio and the compiled player ~/.cache/voce/

voce respects XDG_STATE_HOME and XDG_CACHE_HOME. The cache is safe to delete at any time.

A place is named by a hash of the document's text, not its path, so the same file resumes wherever it is. With --sync the state directory is a git repository; without it, VOCE_STATE can point it at a folder that iCloud Drive, Dropbox or Syncthing carries between computers. Two machines reading different documents never touch the same file.

How it works

voce parses Markdown into blocks of plain text, keeping bold, code and the rest as styled spans over that text. The screen draws the spans, and the voice reads the plain text a sentence at a time. Audio is fetched up to eight sentences ahead on a small thread pool. On macOS a tiny Swift program plays it over a pipe, gapless, and reports its position every 50 milliseconds to time the word highlight; on Linux each sentence is handed to mpv or ffplay. The interface is plain curses, redrawn 25 times a second. docs/architecture.md has the details.

Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome, and so is a coding agent doing the work. The repository is set up for one: AGENTS.md tells Claude Code, Codex or Cursor how voce is laid out, how to test it and what to keep stable, so you can ask for the feature you want and review what comes back.

The easiest place to start is a new language for Code, read aloud, such as C, C++, Scala, Dart, Lua, Perl, R or Elixir: one small file of data in speech/words/ and a few tests. The other good first change is a rule a language still lacks. The tests for these are marked as expected failures (search for xfail in tests/test_words_*.py), for example TypeScript's mapped types, Swift's optionals, Go's pointers and C#'s attributes; each passes once the rule is in speech/code.py. CONTRIBUTING.md has the details.

Licence

How it works

blocks.html_en: voce parses Markdown into blocks of plain text, keeping bold, code and the rest as styled spans over that text. The screen draws the spans, and the voice reads the plain text a sentence at a time. Audio is fetched up to eight sentences ahead on a small thread pool. On macOS a tiny Swift program plays it over a pipe, gapless, and reports its position every 50 milliseconds to time the word highlight; on Linux each sentence is handed to mpv or ffplay. The interface is plain curses, redrawn 25 times a second. docs/architecture.md has the details.

The tests for these are marked as expected failures (search for xfail in tests/test_words_*.py), for example TypeScript's mapped types, Swift's optionals, Go's pointers and C#'s attributes; each passes once the rule is in speech/code.py. It shows the page as it should look, with headings, bold, links, highlighted code and lined-up tables, and reads it the way a person would: the prose as prose, and the code the way a pairing partner says it out loud. You can look away, follow along, or jump around with the keyboard or the mouse.

Coding agents write a lot worth knowing: explanations of a codebase, walkthroughs of a pull request, lessons on a language or a framework. voce lets you listen to it instead of reading it, away from the screen if you like. Ask Claude Code, Codex or any agent to write you something, and press play. It reads any Markdown.

  • Reads code like a pairing partner. '1' === 1 is heard as "the string 1 is identical to 1", and $totals[$channel] ??= 0; as "totals channel null coalescing assignment zero". Operators get their manual's real names, in each language's own words, so you learn to say them. Thirteen languages so far: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust, PHP, Ruby, Java, C#, Swift, Kotlin, shell and SQL. See Code, read aloud.
  • Reads what a person would read. Markup is never spoken. Tables are read row by row, and links by their text. Things meant for the eye stay on the screen.
  • Follows along. The sentence being read sits on a pale band, and the word being spoken on a darker one. The page scrolls to keep your place, and a click on any sentence jumps there.
  • Knows Claude Code. voce -r reads Claude's latest reply in the folder you are in, with no copying.
  • Keeps your place. Quit at any point and it starts from the same sentence next time, even if the file has changed. It also reloads a file when it changes on disk.
  • Sounds good, costs nothing. Kokoro, a small open voice, runs on your computer out of the box: no account, no key, nothing sent anywhere. Every sentence is made once and cached, so listening again is instant.
  • Goes with you. --export turns files into one MP3 with the same voice and pauses, for a walk or a drive.

比较如何

Text-to-speech isn't new, and nor is having an agent's reply read out. What voce adds is code heard the way a person says it, with the page following along. Here is one line, $totals[$channel] ??= 0;, read four ways:

读者 What you hear On screen
Screen readers (VoiceOver, NVDA, Emacspeak) "dollar totals left bracket dollar channel right bracket question question equals zero semicolon", or the symbols skipped your editor, as it is
Read-aloud apps (Speechify, a browser's read aloud) the code read as prose, so Str::slug becomes "stress log" their own app
Agent read-aloud hooks and plugins usually "code omitted" nothing: audio only
voce "totals channel null coalescing assignment zero" the Markdown, styled, each word lit as it is spoken

voce is not a screen reader, and doesn't try to be one. It is for listening to things worth taking in: an agent's explanation, a pull request walkthrough, study notes on a language.

安装

You need macOS or Linux, and Python 3.10 to 3.14 for Kokoro, the voice that works out of the box. macOS's own python3 is 3.9, which gets only the Mac's voices, so name a newer one when you install (uv fetches it if you don't have it):

uv tool install --python 3.13 voce
# or
pipx install --python python3.13 voce

Then try it:

voce README.md

Two optional extras make it better:

  • The Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install) let voce build its small native audio player the first time it runs. You get gapless playback, a pause that keeps your place mid-word, and a word highlight that stays in time. Without them it falls back to afplay.
  • ffmpeg (brew install ffmpeg) is needed for --export.

On Linux, voce plays audio with mpv or ffplay if one is installed, else with pw-play, paplay or aplay, which play at one speed only. For the clipboard it uses wl-clipboard on Wayland, or xclip or xsel on X11:

sudo apt install mpv wl-clipboard      # or: sudo dnf install mpv wl-clipboard

On Windows, run it in WSL, where it is Linux.

Use it

voce notes.md              # read a file, from where you left off
voce a.md b.md             # read several files in a row
voce -r                    # read Claude Code's latest reply in this folder
voce -c                    # read what is on the clipboard
cat notes.md | voce -      # read standard input
voce                       # carry on with whatever you were last reading
voce --start notes.md      # start again from the top
voce notes.md --export notes.mp3   # one MP3 to take with you
voce --check notes.md      # how it will read: sentences, minutes, characters

A click on a sentence or a line of code jumps to it. Drag across any text to copy it, without moving the voice: it is on the clipboard when you let go. With --skip-code, a click on a code block copies it. To select text with the terminal's own mouse instead, hold shift while you drag.

The mouse wheel scrolls, and the page follows the voice again at the next sentence. Vim users can use h j k l.

Every reader that speaks code gets it wrong in one of two ways. Screen readers read the symbols one by one: "dollar, totals, left bracket, dollar, channel...". Text-to-speech apps read code as if it were prose, and Str::slug comes out as "stress log". Neither says what a colleague sitting next to you would say.

voce reads code the way a pairing partner says it out loud, one line at a time, and the line sits on the band as it is read, with the word being spoken marked, just like a sentence of prose.

The rules are the ones a person uses without thinking. Names are said as words: strlen is "string length", isset is "is set" and checkIn is "check In". Dollar signs, brackets and semicolons are silent. A string is read by its contents, so '' is "the empty string", and comments and doc comments are read as prose.

Operators get the names their language's manual gives them: PHP's === is "is identical to", not "triple equals", JavaScript's is "is strictly equal to", Go's := is "short variable declaration", Rust's ::< is "turbofish" and Kotlin's ?: is "elvis". Because the names are the real ones, you learn them as you listen, and they come out of your mouth when you pair or review code.

Each language is one file of words and operator names in speech/words/, naming the manual it follows, with tests that pin the exact words. Each was read through well-known projects in it with docs/hearing/corpus.py and checked by ear against the real voice. A fenced block is read in the language on its fence, a diff in the language of its file, and inline code in the language most of the document's code is in.

If you would rather hear only the prose, --skip-code shows code without reading it.

Use it with Claude Code

Keep Claude Code in one terminal and open a second one in the same folder. When a reply lands, run:

voce -r

voce finds the session for that folder in ~/.claude/projects. It reads the same text that /copy would take, which is Claude's final message without the progress notes, tool calls or thinking. If a turn is still running, it reads the previous reply.

You can also /copy the reply and run voce -c, which works in any terminal and with any tool.

Voices

Kokoro works out of the box. It is a small open voice model that runs on your computer, so it is free, needs no account and sends nothing anywhere. The first time it speaks, voce downloads the model (120 MB) into its cache. It needs Python 3.10 to 3.14; on 3.9, voce uses the Mac's own voices instead (on Linux, install a newer Python).

The Mac's voices are always there on macOS: voce --mac, or voce --mac --voice Daniel to pick one. Add better ones in System Settings, under Accessibility, Spoken Content, System voice, Manage voices.

Press v to move through an engine's voices and V to move to the other engine; both are remembered. Or name a voice and the engine follows: --voice bm_george (Kokoro) or --voice Daniel (the Mac). --engine picks an engine outright. If Kokoro fails part-way through, voce reads that sentence with the Mac's voice and tells you why. The full guide is in docs/voices.md.

Playlists and quizzes

A playlist is a README with a ## Listen in this order section that lists Markdown files, grouped into parts:

## Listen in this order

### Part 1. The basics
1. [Getting started](basics/start.md) · 12 min
2. [Core ideas](basics/ideas.md) · 9 min

Run voce --playlist path/to/folder once. After that, voce works through the files in order, voce --menu lets you choose one, and voce --list shows your progress. voce --prepare 1 fetches the audio for part 1 ahead of time, and voce --minutes updates the "· N min" figures.

A file with a numbered list under ## Quiz and the same number of answers under ## Answers becomes a quiz. voce reads a question, waits while you answer out loud, and reads the answer when you press space. voce --quiz runs just the quizzes. See docs/playlists.md.

What it understands

Headings, paragraphs, bold, italic, struck-through text, inline code, links and images all work. So do nested, numbered and task lists, block quotes and rules. Fenced code blocks are highlighted for every language Pygments knows, and long lines wrap instead of being cut off. Tables line up in columns, respect column alignment, and are read one row at a time.

It also handles a few things that suit listening. Anything inside <details> is shown but not read. Lines that are only links, such as breadcrumbs or "Next:" links, are shown but not read. Symbols such as →, ≈ and ×, and abbreviations such as "e.g." and "i.e.", are read as words.

Code, in fenced blocks and in sentences, is read the way a pairing partner says it: see Code, read aloud. A fenced diff block is highlighted with added lines in the file's syntax and removed lines in red, and read hunk by hunk: "Line 40", then the changed lines, with "Added" and "Removed" said once at the start of each run and the unchanged context shown but not read. Write the file's language after the word diff, as in ```diff python, to have the added lines highlighted and read in that language.

Pick up on another device

voce --sync you/voce keeps your places, settings and a prepared copy of each document in a private git repository of your own, so a second computer carries on where the first left off. A web app reads the same repository on a phone or in any browser, with a voice that runs in the page. There is no voce service: the repository is yours. See docs/sync.md.

隐私

voce has no telemetry and makes no network calls of its own. What you read never leaves your computer: the only download is the Kokoro model, once, from GitHub. Everything voce keeps stays on your computer:

What Where
Your place in each document, one small file per document ~/.local/state/voce/places/
Speed, engine, voices and playlist ~/.local/state/voce/settings.json
Documents prepared for other devices ~/.local/state/voce/prepared/
The last 50 clipboard, reply and piped texts ~/.local/state/voce/clips/
Cached audio and the compiled player ~/.cache/voce/

voce respects XDG_STATE_HOME and XDG_CACHE_HOME. The cache is safe to delete at any time.

A place is named by a hash of the document's text, not its path, so the same file resumes wherever it is. With --sync the state directory is a git repository; without it, VOCE_STATE can point it at a folder that iCloud Drive, Dropbox or Syncthing carries between computers. Two machines reading different documents never touch the same file.

它是如何运作的

voce parses Markdown into blocks of plain text, keeping bold, code and the rest as styled spans over that text. The screen draws the spans, and the voice reads the plain text a sentence at a time. Audio is fetched up to eight sentences ahead on a small thread pool. On macOS a tiny Swift program plays it over a pipe, gapless, and reports its position every 50 milliseconds to time the word highlight; on Linux each sentence is handed to mpv or ffplay. The interface is plain curses, redrawn 25 times a second. docs/architecture.md has the details.

贡献

Issues and pull requests are welcome, and so is a coding agent doing the work. The repository is set up for one: AGENTS.md tells Claude Code, Codex or Cursor how voce is laid out, how to test it and what to keep stable, so you can ask for the feature you want and review what comes back.

The easiest place to start is a new language for Code, read aloud, such as C, C++, Scala, Dart, Lua, Perl, R or Elixir: one small file of data in speech/words/ and a few tests. The other good first change is a rule a language still lacks. The tests for these are marked as expected failures (search for xfail in tests/test_words_*.py), for example TypeScript's mapped types, Swift's optionals, Go's pointers and C#'s attributes; each passes once the rule is in speech/code.py. CONTRIBUTING.md has the details.
